question: When is a person said to 'make a false document' under Section 335 of the BNS? Explain with Illustrations.
modelAnswer: Section 335 (formerly s.464 IPC) says a person makes a false document or false electronic record in three situations. (A) He dishonestly or fraudulently makes, signs, seals or executes a document or part of it; makes or transmits an electronic record or part of it; affixes an electronic signature on an electronic record; or makes a mark denoting execution or authenticity — intending it to be believed that it was made or authorised by a person who, he knows, did not make or authorise it. Examples: adding a zero to a letter of credit so that ₹10,000 reads ₹1,00,000 (Illustration (a)); affixing Z's seal to a conveyance without authority (Illustration (b)); filling up a signed blank cheque beyond the authorised amount (Illustrations (c), (d)). (B) Without lawful authority, he dishonestly or fraudulently alters a document or electronic record in a material part after it has been made or executed, by himself or anyone else, living or dead — for example scratching a legatee's name out of a will (Illustration (f)). (C) He dishonestly or fraudulently causes a person to sign, seal, execute or alter a document, or affix an electronic signature, knowing that the person, because of unsoundness of mind or intoxication, cannot, or because of deception does not, know its contents or the nature of the alteration — as when A writes a different legatee in a will dictated by Z and induces Z to sign it (Illustration (i)). Explanation 1 provides that signing one's own name may be forgery, where the intent is that it be taken as another person's signature, or where a document is antedated to deceive (Illustrations (a)-(e) to Expl. 1). Explanation 2 covers documents made in the name of a fictitious or deceased person. Explanation 3 adopts the IT Act meaning of 'affixing electronic signature'. Section 335 is only a definition; forgery and its punishment are in s.336.

question: Define forgery under Section 336 and explain the graded punishments.
modelAnswer: Under s.336(1) (formerly s.463 IPC), whoever makes a false document or false electronic record, or part of one, with intent (i) to cause damage or injury to the public or any person, (ii) to support any claim or title, (iii) to cause any person to part with property, (iv) to cause any person to enter into an express or implied contract, or (v) to commit fraud or that fraud may be committed, commits forgery. Its two elements are therefore: a false document within s.335, and one of these specified intents. The punishments are: (2) forgery — imprisonment of either description up to two years, or fine, or both (non-cognizable, bailable); (3) forgery intending the forged document to be used for cheating — up to seven years and fine (cognizable, non-bailable); (4) forgery intending, or knowing it likely, that the document will harm the reputation of any party — up to three years and fine (cognizable, bailable). All are triable by a Magistrate of the first class. Heavier punishments apply depending on the type of document forged: s.337 (court records, public registers, Government ID documents, official certificates, powers of attorney) up to seven years; s.338 (valuable securities, wills, adoption authorities, receipts) life or up to ten years. The BNS combines the definition and punishments that the IPC had spread over ss.463, 465, 468 and 469.

question: Distinguish between forgery (Section 336) and cheating (Section 318). Can they overlap?
modelAnswer: Forgery concerns the making of a false document or electronic record with one of the intents in s.336(1); cheating concerns deceiving a person and thereby inducing him to deliver property or to act or omit to his harm. (1) Act: forgery requires making a false document (s.335); cheating requires deception, which may be by words, conduct or documents. (2) Completion: forgery is complete when the false document is made with the required intent, even if never used and no one is deceived; cheating requires that someone is actually deceived and induced. (3) Victim: forgery need not have a victim who has been harmed; cheating requires a person deceived. (4) Punishment: forgery two years (basic); cheating three years (basic), seven years under s.318(4). The two frequently overlap. Where a person forges a document intending to use it to cheat, s.336(3) applies (seven years), and if he then uses it and actually cheats someone, he may be charged with forgery for cheating (s.336(3)), using the forged document as genuine (s.340), and cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property (s.318(4)). For example, a person who forges a sale deed of another's land and uses it to take an advance from a buyer commits all three offences.

question: Explain Sections 337 and 338 of the BNS. What change has been made in Section 337?
modelAnswer: Both provide aggravated punishment for forgery according to the kind of document forged. Section 337 (formerly s.466 IPC) punishes forgery of a document or electronic record purporting to be a record or proceeding of or in a Court; an identity document issued by Government, including a voter identity card or Aadhaar card; a register of birth, marriage or burial; a register kept by a public servant; a certificate or document purporting to be made by a public servant in his official capacity; an authority to institute or defend a suit, take proceedings in it or confess judgment; or a power of attorney. The punishment is imprisonment of either description up to seven years and fine; it is non-cognizable, non-bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. Its Explanation defines 'register' to include any list, data or record maintained in electronic form (as defined in the IT Act). The change is the express inclusion of Government identity documents such as voter ID and Aadhaar, reflecting the widespread misuse of fake identity documents. Section 338 (formerly s.467 IPC) punishes forgery of a document purporting to be a valuable security, a will, an authority to adopt a son, an authority to make or transfer a valuable security or receive its principal, interest or dividends, an authority to receive or deliver money, movable property or a valuable security, or an acquittance or receipt for money, movable property or a valuable security. Because these documents directly create or transfer property rights, the punishment is imprisonment for life, or up to ten years, and fine. It is non-cognizable (cognizable where the valuable security is a Central Government promissory note), non-bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class.

question: Explain the offences of possessing and using forged documents under Sections 339 and 340.
modelAnswer: Section 340(1) defines a forged document or electronic record: a false document or electronic record made wholly or in part by forgery. Section 340(2) (formerly s.471 IPC) punishes whoever fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any document or electronic record which he knows or has reason to believe to be forged; he is punished in the same manner as if he had forged it. So the person using a forged will faces the s.338 punishment, and the person using a forged Aadhaar card the s.337 punishment. The user need not be the forger. The offence is cognizable, bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. Section 339 (formerly s.474 IPC) punishes possession: whoever has in his possession a document or electronic record, knowing it to be forged and intending that it shall fraudulently or dishonestly be used as genuine, is punishable — if it is a document of the kind described in s.337, with up to seven years and fine; if of the kind described in s.338, with life imprisonment or up to seven years and fine. Here no use is required; possession with knowledge and intent completes the offence. Together these sections reach everyone in the chain: the forger (ss.336-338), the person who keeps forged documents ready for use (s.339), and the person who uses them (s.340).

question: What is falsification of accounts under Section 344?
modelAnswer: Section 344 (formerly s.477A IPC) punishes a clerk, officer or servant, or a person employed or acting in that capacity, who wilfully and with intent to defraud: (a) destroys, alters, mutilates or falsifies any book, electronic record, paper, writing, valuable security or account that belongs to or is in the possession of his employer, or has been received by him for or on behalf of his employer; or (b) makes, or abets the making of, any false entry in such a book, record or account, or omits or alters, or abets the omission or alteration of, any material particular in it. The punishment is imprisonment of either description up to seven years, or fine, or both; it is non-cognizable, bailable and triable by a Magistrate of the first class. The Explanation makes prosecution easier: it is enough to allege a general intent to defraud, without naming the particular person to be defrauded, the particular sum, or the particular day. The section targets employees who manipulate their employer's records — for example, cashiers who enter fictitious withdrawals or accountants who suppress receipts — and it expressly covers electronic records. Such conduct often also amounts to criminal breach of trust (s.316) or forgery.

question: What is a 'property mark'? Explain the offences relating to property marks.
modelAnswer: Under s.345(1) (formerly s.479 IPC), a property mark is a mark used for denoting that movable property belongs to a particular person — for example, a brand on cattle or a name stencilled on sacks or crates. The offences are: (1) Using a false property mark (s.345(2)-(3)): marking goods or their container, or using a marked container, in a manner reasonably calculated to cause belief that the goods belong to someone to whom they do not belong — up to one year, or fine, or both, unless the accused proves he acted without intent to defraud. (2) Tampering with a property mark (s.346): removing, destroying, defacing or adding to it, intending or knowing it likely to cause injury — up to one year, or fine, or both. (3) Counterfeiting a property mark (s.347): of another person — up to two years, or fine, or both; of a public servant, or a public servant's mark of manufacture, quality, passage through an office or exemption, or using such a counterfeit mark as genuine — up to three years and fine. (4) Making or possessing instruments for counterfeiting a property mark, or possessing a property mark to falsely denote ownership (s.348) — up to three years, or fine, or both. (5) Selling, exposing or possessing for sale goods with a counterfeit property mark (s.349) — up to one year, or fine, or both, unless the seller proves reasonable precautions and disclosure of his supplier, or that he otherwise acted innocently. (6) Making or using a false mark on a package to misrepresent its contents (s.350) — up to three years, or fine, or both, unless he proves no intent to defraud. All are non-cognizable and bailable. Sections 345(3), 347(1) and 349 are compoundable by the person suffering loss or injury. Several of these place the burden of proof on the accused.

question: Problem: After his father's death, A finds his father's registered will leaving the family house to A's sister. A destroys it, prepares a new 'will' leaving the house to himself, traces his father's signature on it, and files it in court to obtain probate. Discuss A's liability.
modelAnswer: Destroying the genuine will: A fraudulently and dishonestly, and with intent to cause injury to his sister, destroyed a document that is a will. This is the offence under s.343 — imprisonment for life, or up to seven years, and fine; non-cognizable, non-bailable. Making the new will: by writing a will and tracing his father's signature, A dishonestly made a document intending it to be believed that it was signed by his father, who he knows did not sign it — a false document under s.335(A). He made it to support a claim to the house and to injure his sister, so it is forgery under s.336(1). Since the document purports to be a will, the aggravated offence under s.338 applies — imprisonment for life, or up to ten years, and fine. Using it in court: by filing the forged will to obtain probate, A fraudulently used as genuine a document he knew to be forged, punishable under s.340(2) in the same manner as forging it (i.e., as under s.338). A may also be liable in Chapter XIV for fabricating false evidence (s.228) and corruptly using evidence known to be false (s.233), since he produced the forged will in a judicial proceeding, and for knowingly making a false claim in court (s.246). The court before which the forged will is produced would normally file a complaint for prosecution.

question: Can a person commit forgery by signing his own name? Explain.
modelAnswer: Yes. Explanation 1 to s.335 states that a man's signature of his own name may amount to forgery. The key is not whose name is signed, but whether the document is dishonestly or fraudulently made to appear to be something it is not. The Illustrations to Explanation 1 show this: (a) A signs his own name to a bill of exchange intending it to be believed that the bill was drawn by another person of the same name — forgery; (c) A picks up a bill payable to the order of a different person of the same name and endorses it in his own name, intending it to be believed that the payee endorsed it — forgery; (d) a judgment-debtor who, after seizure of his estate, executes a lease in his own name but antedates it to before the seizure, to defraud the purchaser — forgery by antedating; (e) a trader facing insolvency who writes a promissory note in his own name and antedates it to defraud creditors — forgery. In each case the document falsely represents the identity of the person who made it, or the time at which it was made, and is made dishonestly or fraudulently — which is what s.335 requires. Merely putting one's own signature on a document containing false statements is not forgery unless it falls within one of the clauses of s.335.
